transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

With all the changes at work and at home, I just can’t seem to get my feet back under me or handle things the way I used to. It feels like everything shifted at once, and I'm just struggling to keep up.
Have you been feeling down or lost interest in things you usually enjoy, even when there aren’t any obvious stressors around?

I've definitely pulled back and lost interest in things I used to love, like church, woodworking, and fishing trips with my buddies. But it doesn't feel random—it's directly tied to all these massive changes at work and the house being so quiet. If those stressors were to settle down, I honestly think I'd feel like my old self and get right back to them.
Even if the stress at work and home were to improve, do you think your low mood and lack of interest would lift right away, or do you feel they’ve taken on a life of their own?

I definitely think they would lift. If I could go back to my old rural schedule or if things at home felt more like they used to, I'd expect this rough patch to ease up within a few months. It doesn't feel like it has a life of its own, it's just completely tied to these specific changes.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["F43", "F32"], but based on this conversation, F32 (depressive episode) seems less likely because the patient explicitly links their low mood and loss of interest directly to identifiable psychosocial stressors and believes symptoms would resolve if those stressors improved. There is no indication of persistent, endogenous depression independent of the stressors, which makes an adjustment disorder (F43) more consistent with the clinical picture. The absence of symptoms persisting beyond the expected reaction to stress or taking on a life of their own argues against a primary mood disorder.

There is no indication of an independent depressive syndrome, and the symptoms are best explained as a prolonged adjustment reaction with depressed mood.
